competitive_moat.rationale: Mixed, segment-dependent picture from FY2025 10-K + market data, not a clean pass on the rubric cross-checks. (a) Pricing power: real but uneven -- Domestic Disney+ ARPU +2.2% (below recent CPI), International ARPU +19% (strong), Parks guest spending +3%. (b) Margin vs. industry median: not evidenced (Entertainment op income +19% on +3% revenue shows leverage but no peer benchmark found). (c) Retention/switching costs: not evidenced beyond strategic intent (Iger calling the Disney+/Hulu bundle "the strategic moat"); no churn/retention data gathered. (d) Market share: NEGATIVE for streaming specifically -- Disney+ ~14% US SVOD share, 4th place, explicitly described as trailing Netflix's widening dominance; Parks/IP franchise strength is real but not quantified here. Only 1 of 4 cross-checks (pricing power) has clear positive evidence strong enough to count; rubric requires 2+ for a 4/5. Scored 3 (mild moat, contestable) rather than 4 given the streaming-share evidence actively cuts against, not just fails to support, the case. Sourced from Disney FY2025 10-K (SEC EDGAR, filed 2025-11-13) plus 2026 streaming-market-share industry writeups (evoca.tv, matrixbcg.com) and commentary (Yahoo Finance, Kavout).

revenue_visibility.rationale: FY2025 10-K segment mix (SEC EDGAR, filed 2025-11-13): Linear Networks $9,364M (9.9% of $94,425M total; genuinely contracted -- multi-year MVPD affiliate-fee agreements at contractually specified per-subscriber rates) + Direct-to-Consumer $24,614M (26.1%; recurring subscription revenue, but month-to-month/cancel-anytime, not contracted in the strict sense) = ~36% of company revenue is contracted-or-recurring. Content Sales/Licensing (9.0%) and Experiences (38.3%, mostly transactional ticket/spend) are not visible 12 months out. Sports segment (16.7%, not broken out here) likely has some ESPN affiliate-contract component similar to Linear Networks, which could push the true figure into the 3 band (40-60%) if isolated -- this is a boundary call between bands 2 and 3, scored conservatively at 2 given the Sports-segment split was not available in the evidence gathered. Flag for Alan: worth pulling the Sports segment 10-K detail to firm this up before finalizing.

competitive_moat.rationale: Clears all four rubric cross-checks with real, sourced evidence. (a) Pricing power: March 2026 price hike (Premium to $26.99/mo) with JPMorgan/Citi projecting ~$1.7B annualized revenue lift -- pricing power without volume loss, by analyst consensus. (b) Margin vs. peers: 2026 operating margin guided to 31.5% (up from 29.5% in 2025, itself +3pp YoY) -- the highest operating margin of any major pure-play streaming service, per the company's own Q4 2025 shareholder letter (content amortization growing ~10% vs. revenue growth of 12-14%). (c) Retention/switching costs: the password-sharing crackdown (global by end-2024) added 23M+ net subscribers over the following year against a projected 10-20% household churn; resubscribe rates among affected households now exceed 40% -- real, tested evidence of low switching despite an actively imposed friction. (d) Market share: 325M+ global subscribers, more than double Disney+ (~132M), with average U.S. watch time over 1hr/day vs. 36min for the next-closest competitor (Hulu). Scored 5 (wide moat, multiple reinforcing advantages) at Medium rather than High confidence because the market-share and retention evidence, while consistent across sources, comes from independent research/analytics writeups rather than audited filings -- only the margin data is primary-source (company shareholder letter).

revenue_visibility.rationale: Revenue is essentially all subscription-based with no meaningful separate licensing/wholesale line (unlike DIS). Not literally "contracted" -- subscriptions are month-to-month, cancel-anytime -- so not scored a 5. But practical visibility is high: the ability of JPMorgan/Citi to project a precise ~$1.7B revenue lift from a specific March 2026 price change implies a highly stable, low-churn, predictable subscriber base in aggregate. Scored 4 (60-80% band) as the better fit than a literal-contracts reading would suggest, given the rubric explicitly allows "recurring" alongside "contracted" revenue. This is a judgment call on how strictly to read "contracted" for a subscription (vs. contract-locked) business -- worth Alan's explicit view before finalizing. Sourced from Netflix Q4 2025 shareholder letter (company IR) and 2026 price-increase analyst coverage (CNBC, JPMorgan/Citi via FinancialContent).
